title: Compile ahead. Interpret each form. JIT both.
lede: AOT (C, Go, rustc): translate to machine code before run; 0 warmup, platform-specific binary. Interpreter (CPython bytecode loop, early Java): execute forms one by one; portable, slow. JIT (V8, HotSpot, LuaJIT): interpret/baseline, then compile hot loops to native with types you observed.
diagram: Box1 gcc -O2 → ELF. Box2 CPython: .pyc, ceval.c loop ~10–100× C. Box3 V8: Ignition then TurboFan on hot functions. Caption: Graal, Pypy, JavaScriptCore same shape.
what: When the machine code is produced. JIT needs warmup and can deoptimize if types change.
why: Why Python is slow in a tight loop and C isn’t. Why JVM needs -XX:… and a 30s warm bench.
trap: Benchmarking JIT with one iteration. Shipping an interpreter in a 1 ms p99 path. Assuming ‘compiled’ means optimized (gcc -O0).

title: Bytecode is a portable ISA.
lede: Bytecode is instructions for a virtual machine, not for your CPU. javac → .class (stack machine). CPython → .pyc. WASM → a linear-memory ISA in the browser/edge. The VM maps those ops to native (interpret or JIT). One artifact, many CPUs.
diagram: Left: x86_64 ELF, won’t run on ARM. Right: .class / wasm, VM on each. facts: JVM iadd; Python LOAD_FAST; WASM i32.add. Caption: .pyc is version-locked to CPython.
what: Stable, simpler ISA + a runtime. Verification (JVM, WASM) can reject illegal programs before run.
why: Portability and sandboxing. Android ART, Spark, the browser.
trap: Shipping .pyc across Python minor versions. Treating WASM as ‘C speed’ without noticing bounds checks and the JS glue.

title: The linker resolves names to addresses.
lede: cc -c produces .o with reloc holes: call printf is ‘undefined’. ld (or lld, link.exe) concatenates .o/.a, assigns addresses, patches relocs, emits the executable or .so. Dynamic linking delays some resolution to load (PLT/GOT).
diagram: 1 compile units. 2 archive .a is a pile of .o. 3 undefined symbol → linker error, not a runtime NameError (unless dynamic). Caption: --as-needed, LTO is link-time optimize.
what: Name → address after compile. Static: all in the binary. Dynamic: libfoo.so at load (plate 371).
why: ‘Undefined reference to foo’ is ld, not cc. Order of .a on the command line still matters for some linkers.
trap: Assuming a header ‘links’ the library — it only declares. Circular .a needing --start-group. Mixing libc++ and libstdc++.

title: ABI is which register is arg0.
lede: Application Binary Interface: sizes, alignment, who saves which register, how a struct is returned, how syscalls look. SysV AMD64: arg0=rdi, 1=rsi, 2=rdx, 3=rcx, 4=r8, 5=r9, rest stack; return rax. Win64: rcx rdx r8 r9. Mix two ABIs in one process = corruption.
diagram: Left SysV: rdi=fd for write. Right Win64: rcx=fd. facts: 8-byte stack align; 16-byte before call on SysV. Caption: extern "C" kills C++ name mangling, not the register contract.
what: The calling convention + type layout. Compilers on one platform agree so .o files combine (plate 325).
why: FFI, assembly, kernel ABI vs user. Why a C library from MSVC may not link with MinGW.
trap: Passing a Go string (ptr+len) to a C char* as if it were one pointer. Forgetting the stack alignment and crashing in XMM.

title: UB is a license, not a crash.
lede: Undefined behavior in C/C++: the standard imposes no requirements. The compiler may delete the branch, format your disk in theory, or ‘work’ until -O2. Signed overflow, use-after-free, data races, out-of-bounds — not a guaranteed SIGSEGV.
diagram: Left: if (p) *p; p proven non-null by an earlier deref the compiler saw — the check vanishes. Right: rust/Go/Java define many of these as panics or wrap. Caption: -fsanitize=undefined, address.
what: A hole in the spec the optimizer exploits. Nasal demons is the joke; deleted checks are the reality.
why: Security (RCE from a ‘benign’ overflow). Why sanitizers exist.
trap: Testing -O0 and shipping -O3. ‘It works on my compiler.’ Using signed i++ to loop to INT_MAX.

title: A static type is checked before run.
lede: Static: the compiler (or typechecker) proves well-typedness using annotations or inference. Illegal programs do not build. Dynamic (Python, JS, Ruby): tags exist at run; errors are exceptions. Gradual (TypeScript): erase to JS — the runtime does not enforce TS types.
diagram: Left: String s = 3; // error at javac. Right: s = 3 in Python; fails when used as str. Caption: TS: compile green, runtime still 3.
what: When the check happens. Erasure (Java generics, TS) means the VM may not know T.
why: API contracts, refactoring, fewer class of bugs. Cost: expressiveness, compile time.
trap: Trusting TypeScript as a runtime check. any everywhere. Thinking Java generics reify T (they don’t, mostly).

title: A dynamic type is a tag at run.
lede: CPython: every value is PyObject* with ob_type. 1+1 looks up nb_add. Cache (specializer in 3.11+) makes the common path shorter, not typed. Boxing: a 64-bit int is a heap object unless interned. That’s the 10–100× vs C.
diagram: 1 PyLong_FromLong(3). 2 BINARY_OP add. 3 type check, unbox, add, box. Caption: JS: tagged pointers (NaN-box or smi). Lua: tagged union.
what: Values carry their operations. Open-world: new types at runtime.
why: Why Python feels fast for I/O (the kernel dominates) and slow for inner loops.
trap: Microbenchmarking Python arithmetic against C. Monkey-patching as architecture.

title: Acquire sees the store. Relaxed does not.
lede: Atomics without a mutex still need an order. relaxed: atomicity only. acquire load: sees all stores before the matching release store. seq_cst: a global order, slowest. x86 is TSO — many orders compile to the same instruction; ARM/RISC-V do not.
diagram: Left: flag relaxed=1; data=42 — reader may see flag and stale data on ARM. Right: store data; release flag; acquire flag; load data. Caption: Java volatile ≈ acquire/release. Go happens-before via channel send.
what: A data race on non-atomics is UB in C++ (plate 327). Atomics + wrong order is a silent stale read.
why: Lock-free flags, once flags, message passing without mutex.
trap: Copying an x86-only mental model to ARM (phones, Apple silicon, Graviton). Using volatile as a mutex (plate 331).

title: volatile is for MMIO, not mutexes.
lede: C volatile: every access hits memory, no reorder by the compiler vs other volatiles — for device registers that change without the compiler knowing. It is not atomic, not a barrier for other threads. Java volatile is a different word (visibility).
diagram: Left (wrong): volatile int flag as a spinlock. Right: atomic_int / std::atomic / mutex; MMIO: *(volatile uint32_t*)0x40001000. Caption: MSVC / C++ have more flags. Use atomics.
what: Compiler I/O to a location. Threading needs atomics or locks (plate 74).
why: Drivers, embedded. The #1 C concurrency misconception.
trap: Porting Java volatile to C. Signaling a thread with a plain bool on ARM.

title: The compiler inserts padding for alignment.
lede: struct { char c; int32 x; } is 8 bytes, not 5: 3 pad so x sits at offset 4 (plate 320). Order fields decreasing size to shrink. packed attribute removes pad and may split loads. JSON/protobuf do not use C layout.
diagram: Left: c, pad, x → 8. Right: x, c, pad → 8 still (struct align is max member). facts: sizeof, alignof, offsetof. 64-bit pointer = 8. Caption: Java/Go reorder; C does not.
what: ABI layout. Array of structs multiplies padding.
why: Wire vs in-memory. Cache-line packing (plate 309).
trap: fwrite(&struct) as a file format. memcmp structs with padding (garbage bytes).

title: null is a pointer. undefined is a JS hole.
lede: C NULL: pointer 0, dereference UB. Java/Go nil/null: typed nothing, NPE/panic on method. JS: undefined = missing binding/property; null = intentional empty; == equal, === not (plate 67). Option/Maybe is a type that forces a check.
diagram: Box1 C *p=0; *p UB. Box2 Optional.ofNullable. Box3 JS x.y if x undefined → TypeError. Caption: SQL NULL is three-valued logic, not a pointer.
what: Absence encodings differ by language. Don’t mix them in APIs (JSON null vs omit).
why: The billion-dollar mistake is preventable with types (plate 328) or checks.
trap: typeof null === 'object' in JS. Using 0 as both integer zero and ‘missing’ in C APIs.

title: JS length is UTF-16 code units.
lede: JavaScript strings are UTF-16. 'é'.length is 1. Many emoji are two units (surrogate pair): '🙂'.length === 2. str[i] is a code unit, not a grapheme. [...str] or for (const c of str) iterates code points. Bytes on the wire are UTF-8 (plate 322).
diagram: Left: .length on emoji. Right: Array.from(s) or Intl.Segmenter for graphemes. Caption: Java String is the same UTF-16 history. Rust str is UTF-8 bytes.
what: Indexing and length are in 16-bit units. Network and files are usually UTF-8.
why: Tweet-sized limits, substr bugs, slicing mid-surrogate producing unpaired values.
trap: s.substring(0, 1) on a leading surrogate. Buffer.byteLength vs string.length in Node.

title: Exceptions unwind. Result is a value.
lede: throw walks frames until catch, running destructors/finally. Cost is on the throw path (and sometimes prevents inlining). Result/Either is a tagged value you match; nothing unwinds. errno is a thread-local int after a C call. Pick one policy per layer.
diagram: Box1 try { foo() } catch. Box2 rust Result, Go (val, err). Box3 C -1 + errno. Caption: exceptions for rare; Result for expected failure (file not found).
what: Control-flow vs data. Mixing them (catching to convert to Result) is a boundary.
why: API design. Why Go doesn’t have exceptions. Why a thrown 404 in a hot parser is a problem.
trap: Using exceptions for every missing map key. Swallowing catch (Exception e) {}. Ignoring errno after a -1.

title: JIT compiles the hot path and may undo it.
lede: V8/HotSpot: count calls, record types (this + is always Smi / HiddenClass H). When hot, compile a specialized native version. If a new type appears, deoptimize back to interpreter/baseline and maybe recompile. That’s why warmup exists and why megamorphic call sites stay slow.
diagram: 1 interpret. 2 10k hits, types stable. 3 native. 4 unexpected class → deopt. Caption: hidden classes / shapes in JS; CHA in Java.
what: Speculative native code. Correctness via deopt. Polymorphism kills the spec.
why: Why the first request is slow. Why a megamorphic interface in a hot Java loop loses inlining.
trap: Benchmarking without warmup. Changing shapes every iteration (obj.k = i random keys). Passing many unexpected types ‘just in case’ through a hot function.

title: A B+ tree is wide and short. Leaves hold rows.
lead: A B+ tree is wide and short.
lede: B-tree / B+ tree: each node is a page (4–8 KiB). Fanout hundreds of keys. Height 3–4 for 1e9 rows. Internal nodes: keys + child pointers. B+: all rows in linked leaves → range scan is a walk, not a tree dance. Postgres btree is this (plate 2).
diagram: Left binary tree height 30 for 1e9. Right B+ height 4, 100-way. facts: 8 KiB page, ~100–300 keys/page depending on key size. Caption: random UUID keys (plate 348) randomize leaf splits.
what: Disk-friendly search tree. Point lookup: height I/Os. Range: height + leaf chain.
why: Why indexes aren’t binary trees in RAM textbooks. Why key size matters (fanout).
trap: A 2 KiB JSON key in the index — fanout collapses, height grows, cache dies.

title: Postgres reads 8 KiB pages, not rows.
lede: Heap and indexes are arrays of 8192-byte pages (BLCKSZ). A seq scan is page I/O. shared_buffers is the cache of pages (often 25% RAM). A row lives in a page with ItemId; updates leave a new tuple version (plate 96, 351).
diagram: facts: 8 KiB; max row ~2 KiB toasts; work_mem per sort; shared_buffers vs OS page cache. TOAST for wide values. Caption: EXPLAIN BUFFERS shows hits/reads (plate 98).
what: I/O unit is the page. Row count is a consequence. Fillfactor leaves air for HOT (plate 350).
why: Tuning, bloat, why random updates hurt more than appends.
trap: shared_buffers = all RAM (no OS cache, no connections). Counting rows as I/O.

title: Seq scan is n pages. Index is log n then heap.
accent: Index is log n then heap.
lede: Seq scan: read every heap page, ~1–2 sequential I/Os per page. Index scan: B+ lookup + one heap fetch per row (random). Planner: cost ≈ pages × random_page_cost (4 on HDD, ~1.1 on SSD). 30% of table? Often seq wins.
diagram: Left: 1e7 rows, 1e5 pages, seq. Right: index 3 page walks + 50 heap pages for 50 rows. Caption: bitmap index scan batches heap fetches (plate 340).
what: The cheaper plan is a function of selectivity and I/O randomness, not ‘index always’.
why: Why an index is unused. Why ANALYZE matters (plate 98).
trap: Index on a boolean 50/50. SELECT * so the index isn’t covering and you heap-fetch anyway.

title: Bitmap AND of two indexes, then heap.
lede: Two moderately selective predicates: Postgres builds a bitmap per index, AND/ORs them, then visits heap pages in order (almost sequential). Cheaper than two index scans that bounce randomly, cheaper than seq if the bitmaps are sparse.
diagram: 1 Bitmap Index Scan idx_a. 2 Bitmap Index Scan idx_b. 3 AND. 4 Bitmap Heap Scan. Caption: lossy bitmaps when work_mem is tight (page-level, extra filter).
what: Combine indexes without a composite (a,b) index. Still not magic if both predicates are 40%.
why: AND of two filters. Why a composite still wins for a,b together (plate 97).
trap: Creating 12 single-column indexes and expecting every AND to be free. Ignoring lossy bitmaps in EXPLAIN.

title: VACUUM marks dead tuples reusable.
lede: MVCC (plate 96): UPDATE/DELETE insert a new version; the old stays until no snapshot can see it. VACUUM (and autovacuum) freeze/mark those ItemIds free. It does not shrink the file unless VACUUM FULL (rewrite). Bloat is dead tuples occupying pages.
diagram: Left: update 1e6 rows, heap 2× until vacuum. Right: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor 0.2. facts: n_dead_tup in pg_stat_user_tables. Caption: index bloat is separate; REINDEX.
what: Garbage collection for tuples. HOT may vacuum a page in-place (plate 350).
why: Table growth after batch updates. Wraparound freeze (plate 342).
trap: Turning autovacuum off. VACUUM FULL on a hot table (exclusive lock). Expecting VACUUM to release bytes to the OS always.

title: Transaction IDs wrap. Freeze is not optional.
lede: Postgres xids are 32-bit. Age > ~2e9 and tuples that are not frozen look in the future — data appears to vanish. VACUUM FREEZE writes frozen xids. autovacuum_freeze_max_age (default 200e6) must run. Monitoring: txid_current(), age(datfrozenxid).
diagram: 1 xid ticks every write tx. 2 freeze old tuples. 3 fail to freeze → wraparound shutdown to protect data. Caption: read-only tx don’t consume xids (in modern PG).
what: A circular counter plus freeze. Operational, not academic.
why: The outage that looks like ‘the table is empty’ or ‘cannot start transactions’.
trap: Long-open transactions blocking freeze. Ignoring wraparound warnings. A replica that never vacuums.

title: Checkpoint flushes dirty pages. WAL already is durable.
lede: WAL (plate 95) is the durability path: commit = fsync WAL. Dirty heap pages sit in shared_buffers until a checkpoint writes them, then WAL before that point can be recycled. checkpoint_timeout 5min, max_wal_size. A spike of writes at checkpoint hurts.
diagram: Left: every commit fsyncs heap — death. Right: commit fsyncs WAL; checkpoint spreads heap writes. Caption: full_page_writes after a checkpoint.
what: Two clocks: WAL insert, checkpoint redo LSN. Crash: replay WAL from last checkpoint.
why: Latency spikes every 5 minutes. Tuning max_wal_size vs timeout.
trap: checkpoint_completion_target 0 and a 30s I/O storm. Disabling full_page_writes on a filesystem without torn-page protection.

title: Physical ships pages. Logical ships rows.
lede: Physical/streaming: replica is the same bytes (block-for-block), same major version, read-only hot standby. Logical: decode WAL to row events, apply to another schema/version, selective tables. Logical is for CDC, upgrades, heterogeneous. Physical is for HA.
diagram: Left physical: primary WAL → replica replay. Right logical: publication → slot → subscriber INSERT/UPDATE. Caption: slots retain WAL until consumed — a stuck slot fills disk.
what: Same-cluster clone vs event stream of rows. Both can lag (plate 99).
why: HA vs integration (Debezium, plate 224).
trap: Logical on a chatty table without a replica identity. A replication slot left behind after dropping a consumer.

title: Partitioning is routing, not a free index.
lede: Declarative partition: parent table, children by RANGE/LIST/HASH of a key. Planner prunes children if the WHERE contains the key. It does not replace an index inside a partition. Attach/detach is why time-series drops old data in O(1) metadata.
diagram: Left: events_2026_08. WHERE ts>='2026-08-01' AND ts<'2026-09-01' → one child. Right: WHERE user_id=7 on a ts-range partition → all children unless you also filter ts. Caption: PK must include the partition key.
what: Constraint-based routing of rows to files. Pruning needs the key in the query.
why: Retention, huge time-series, shard-by-tenant.
trap: 1000s of partitions and no prune (planning time explodes). Unique on (id) without the partition key.

title: max_connections is RAM. Pool in the app.
lede: Each Postgres backend is a process (~5–15 MiB idle + work_mem per sort). 5000 connections = tens of GiB plus context switch death. PgBouncer/ODBC pool (plate 3) in transaction mode. Default max_connections 100 is a hint, not a dare.
diagram: facts: 100 conns; work_mem 4–64 MiB; 100×64 MiB=6.4 GiB if all sort. Caption: RDS ‘max connections’ formulas still want a pooler.
what: Process-per-connection. Multiplex at the pool.
why: The 3am too-many-clients plus OOM. Serverless frontends that open a conn per invoke.
trap: Raising max_connections to match the app server farm. Session-mode pooling with 5k clients anyway.

title: jsonb is binary and indexable. json is text.
lede: json is stored as input text. jsonb is decomposed; whitespace gone; keys unique; GIN indexes path/value. -> returns json; ->> returns text. Prefer jsonb unless you must byte-preserve. Still not a substitute for columns you filter every time.
diagram: Left json: LIKE on a blob. Right jsonb GIN: WHERE extra->>'sku' = 'A1' with expression index. Caption: jsonb_path_ops vs jsonb_ops. TOAST if wide.
what: Typed document in a cell. Index expressions you query.
why: Semi-structured extras. Event payloads.
trap: jsonb for the whole domain model (no constraints, no stats). Updating one key rewrites the TOAST.

title: Random UUIDs as PKs scatter the B+tree.
lede: btree inserts at the rightmost leaf if keys increase (identity, snowflake plate 93, ULID, uuid v7). uuid4 is random: each insert splits a random leaf, dirtying many pages, killing cache. Fine for small tables; painful at 1e8 rows.
diagram: Left uuid4: 16 B key, random leaf. Right bigserial or uuid v7: append. Caption: secondary unique on public id if you need unpredictability (plate 100).
what: Index locality follows key order. Random PKs randomize writes.
why: Write amplification, bloat, checkpoint spikes.
trap: uuid_generate_v4() as PK ‘for security’ on a hot events table. Then clustering on it.

title: INCLUDE makes an index covering without extra sort keys.
lede: A covering index contains every column the query needs → Index Only Scan (visibility map permitting). Extra columns in the key affect sort and uniqueness. INCLUDE (Postgres 11+) stores them in the leaf only. SELECT id, email WHERE email=? → INDEX(email) INCLUDE (id).
diagram: Left INDEX(email, id): uniqueness and order on both. Right INDEX(email) INCLUDE (id): lookup on email, fetch id without heap. Caption: heap fetches if VM bit not set (need VACUUM).
what: Leaf payload vs key. Covering avoids heap I/O.
why: Hot read paths. EXPLAIN Index Only Scan.
trap: Including a 2 KB text column (fat leaves). Expecting Index Only Scan on a never-vacuumed table.

title: HOT updates skip the indexes if indexed cols didn't change.
lead: HOT updates skip the indexes if
lede: If UPDATE does not change any indexed column and there is free space on the page (fillfactor 70–80 on hot tables), Postgres can chain a new tuple on the same page without touching indexes. Else every index on the table gets a new entry — bloat.
diagram: 1 fillfactor=80. 2 UPDATE counter SET n=n+1 WHERE id=1. 3 HOT if id indexes only id. Caption: pg_stat_user_tables n_tup_hot_upd.
what: Page-local new version. Indexes still point at the item id.
why: High-churn rows (counters, locks, sessions). Why an extra index on updated_at hurts.
trap: Indexing a column you UPDATE every time (updated_at). fillfactor 100 on that table.

title: A tuple is (xmin, xmax). Readers see a snapshot.
lede: Heap tuple header: xmin = creating xid, xmax = deleting/updating xid (0 if live). A snapshot is the set of in-progress xids + xmax. The reader sees the version where xmin committed before the snapshot and xmax did not. No row lock for readers (plate 96).
diagram: Left: T1 updates row, T2 SELECT sees old xmin. Right: T1 commit, next snapshot sees new. Caption: HeapTupleSatisfiesMVCC. Long T2 snapshot keeps old versions until T2 ends (bloat, plate 341).
what: Visibility is per-tuple metadata, not a lock. Writers set xmax.
why: READ COMMITTED vs REPEATABLE READ (plate 40) is which snapshot you hold.
trap: A 4-hour report transaction. SELECT FOR UPDATE when you only needed a snapshot.
